summary:
Georgia stands under the national framework that governs every state. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 has required federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F from supporting documents, and passports already carrying an X remain valid until expiry. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and the Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports. A visitor whose documents no longer match their presentation should expect that mismatch to surface at federal checkpoints, where TSA secondary screening, devices and pat-downs can compound the exposure.

Entry and screening follow national rules rather than Georgia law. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sports would be flagged with an internal marking, and applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex can be treated as grounds for a permanent ban on fraud grounds. Several foreign governments, including at least eight European states, adjusted their travel guidance for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States during 2025.

Georgia's own law restricts care rather than entry. Governor Brian Kemp signed Senate Bill 140 on 23 March 2023, barring licensed medical professionals from providing hormone therapy or gender-transition surgery to patients under 18, with licence revocation as a possible penalty; the ban took effect 1 July 2023, and minors who began hormone replacement therapy before that date may continue. The ACLU of Georgia said it would sue. Georgia's public-employee State Health Benefit Plan, by contrast, was required under an October 2023 settlement reached in Atlanta federal court to pay for medically necessary gender-affirming care for employees, spouses and dependents, following a December 2022 discrimination lawsuit; the settlement means the plan could be obliged to cover care for minors outside Georgia even though it is prohibited inside the state.

Adult care access in Georgia has contracted under federal funding pressure. On 13 February 2025 Memorial Health University Medical Center in Savannah cancelled all gender-affirming surgeries, including a pre-approved double mastectomy for a 24-year-old transgender man, citing a responsibility to follow state and federal laws in what appears to reference the 28 January 2025 federal executive order denying Medicare and Medicaid funding to providers of youth gender-transition care. The Current reports the Savannah Pride Center said at least two other area residents were also denied care.

Violence risk is documented and concentrated. Atlanta police said in April 2023 they were actively investigating three violent crimes against transgender women in the city that year, after two Black transgender women were fatally shot a week apart, with a January 2023 shooting that left a transgender woman in critical condition also remaining open; the Atlanta Police Department acknowledged the epidemic-level violence Black and Brown transgender women face in America. Georgia's recorded killing rate for trans women is 4.8 per 100,000 per year, a figure drawn from an undercounted monitoring project and therefore an acknowledged floor rather than a full measure.
tangentialFactors:
Georgia's care ban sits within a national pattern: gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and a July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest state marked "Do Not Travel" for trans people, bringing that total to four. Facilities access is restricted in a growing number of states, with a Movement Advancement Project tally counting state bathroom bans in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, while 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban; in April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, described by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

Document rules are tightening elsewhere as well. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences, invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template for other states. Federal custody also presents documented harm: from 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, and in December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radal gender ideology."
localsOnly:
Georgia residents face a state-level care ban alongside the federal framework. Senate Bill 140, effective 1 July 2023, prohibits licensed medical professionals from providing hormone therapy or gender-transition surgery to patients under 18 and exposes providers to licence revocation, though minors already on hormone replacement therapy before that date may continue.

The State Health Benefit Plan covering Georgia public employees is under a October 2023 federal-court settlement requiring it to pay for medically necessary gender-affirming care for employees, spouses and dependents, a coverage obligation that survived the 2023 state care ban and that could extend to care for minors obtained outside Georgia.

Atlanta carries a documented concentration of lethal violence against transgender women, with three violent-crime investigations open as of April 2023 following two fatal shootings of Black transgender women a week apart and a January 2023 shooting that left a transgender woman in critical condition. The statewide killing rate for trans women is recorded at 4.8 per 100,000 per year, an undercounted floor figure.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the ACLU of Georgia's announced challenge to Senate Bill 140 is unresolved in the available sources; no outcome, dismissal or ruling is sourced here.

Whether the October 2023 State Health Benefit Plan settlement remains in force, has been modified, or has been affected by subsequent state or federal action is not sourced in this inventory.

The 4.8 per 100,000 killing-rate figure derives from an undercounted monitoring project and is presented by its own source as a floor; the true rate is not established.

Georgia-specific enforcement data on federal passport or visa screening, and any Georgia-specific bathroom or facilities restrictions beyond the school and government-building pattern described nationally, are not sourced in this inventory.
